doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: How he starts an arrangement; I Only Have Eyes for You
summary: He starts by writing out melody and chords, and spent three weeks on a Bruno Mars-style arrangement for Joe Bwarie.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Did you ever have a circumstance – you’re talking about writing for a pops orchestra – arranging something you had done years before but you never had to notate and include the melody because someone was singing it? And then you’re writing for a pops orchestra with let’s say a medley and no one is singing, all of a sudden it’s like, “Wow, I never wrote out ‘Sherry Baby’ before, the actual melody of it.”

Well when I wrote the arrangements I always wrote the melody on the top line unless I was sweetening a record where they already had the singer on, where all I had to do was just write the parts. But when I started a session the first thing I do is I write out the melody. I want to know what the melody is, and then I write out the basic chords, and then I’ll change the chords as I go along but I do a basic layout of just the song. Because every time I start an arrangement I start with a blank page. So I’ve recently listened to four albums I did over the past couple of years and I’d say, “How did I come up with this? Where did I get this idea?” And it puzzles me every time I do it. But as I’m writing the melody down there’s things that I’m picking up in my brain as I’m doing it and there’s just, for some reason I think by writing the melody it gives me an opportunity to at least get an idea as to where this thing is going to go. And for some reason there’s a way of putting it together where you don’t have to write the same intro, it’s always different, and you wonder where it’s going to come from but it always seems to come.
Do you have to step away sometimes and go do something else? Go for a walk and let your head work the thing out on its own?

Well I recently did another record with Joe Bwarie which was a lot of fun. And he wanted to do “I Only Have Eyes for You.” And he wanted it to sound like a pop record. And I love Bruno Mars. So I worked on the arrangement for three weeks until I came up with the idea. I worked on the song for three weeks, and I finally came up with it. And I think the record is absolutely sensational, although very few people will hear it. But it was a Bruno Mars’ style. And I also took The Flamingos’ thing, and the way I put it
together it’s a totally different record, different song, but it was something like I said I don’t have it yet.
It wasn’t talking to you yet.

Yeah. It wasn’t saying, “Hey Charlie, it needs this.” But eventually it did. So if you want to get a chance to listen to it, it’s on Joe Bwarie’s “Lucky 13” new album and it’s “I Only Have Eyes for You” now. Then after I made the record, I turned the record over to a synth programmer who took my arrangement and tweaked it and made it in some ways better, in some ways the same, but it’s the essence of the record. Because of all the backgrounds, the lead, the layout, everything – the chord structure, the feel, everything else and it was all me. And I sort of listened to the record and I said, “That was a hard record to make.”
